intro.title: About the park
intro.description:
Parc Municipal de Luxembourg is the historic city park of Luxembourg City, laid out between 1871 and 1878 by the French landscape architect Édouard André on the ramparts left behind after the 1867 Treaty of London ordered the fortress demolished. It is the green heart of Ville-Haute: broad lawns, mature trees, a bandstand area, an orangery, sculpture groups and two villas — Villa Vauban, now an art museum, and Villa Louvigny.

Locals call the big central meadow the Kinnekswiss ("the King's meadow"), and it is where the city holds open-air concerts, the Spillfest children's festival and the summer Kinnekswiss Loves programme. On a normal weekday the park is a place to walk, sit in the shade, let children run in the playgrounds or eat lunch on the grass, five minutes from the shopping streets of the upper town.

visitGuide.title: Good to know before you go
items: Free admission: the park, lawns and playgrounds cost nothing
Weekday mornings and early evenings are quietest; summer weekends on the Kinnekswiss are busy
Paths are mostly level and paved — suitable for pushchairs and wheelchairs
Public transport in Luxembourg is free in standard class, so no ticket is needed for tram or bus
Shade is plentiful under the old trees; bring water on hot summer days

kinnekswiss.title: Kinnekswiss — the King's meadow
kinnekswiss.lead: The Kinnekswiss is the large open lawn at the centre of Parc Municipal. In Luxembourgish the name means "the King's meadow", and it is the park's best-known space: the place people mean when they say "let's meet on the Kinnekswiss".
paragraphs: The meadow sits in the middle of the park, a few minutes' walk from the Bd Joseph II entrance and from Villa Vauban. Because it is flat, open and surrounded by old trees, it works equally well for a picnic, a game of football, a lunch break from the nearby offices, or as standing room at an open-air concert.

The City of Luxembourg uses the Kinnekswiss as one of its main event venues. The summer programme Kinnekswiss Loves brings concerts, screenings and sports activities to the lawn; Spillfest, the free children's play festival, is held here; and winter instalments have included ice rinks and the Wanterpark. Outside event dates the lawn is simply public grass — free to use, no booking.
bullets: Where: centre of Parc Municipal, ~5 min walk from the Bd Joseph II entrance
What: large open lawn with mature trees around the edges
Free: no booking, no fee, open during park hours
Events: Kinnekswiss Loves, Spillfest, winter ice rink and Wanterpark
Getting there: tram T1 to Hamilius or Stäreplaz/Étoile, then 5–10 minutes on foot

knowledge.title: History, landscape and what you will see

sections.title: From fortress rampart to public garden (1871–1878)
sections.content:
After the 1867 Treaty of London, Luxembourg's fortress was dismantled and the ring of ramparts around the upper town became available land. The city decided to turn part of it into a public garden. The French landscape architect Édouard André was commissioned, and the park was laid out between 1871 and 1878, which is why the City of Luxembourg still calls it the "Edouard André Municipal Park".

The park has been adapted several times since: the orangery, the bandstand area, the sculpture groups and the children's playgrounds were added later, and two historic buildings stand inside its perimeter. Villa Louvigny housed the Luxembourg broadcasting company and hosted the Eurovision Song Contest in 1962 and 1966. Villa Vauban, the original seat of the European Court of Justice, is today the city's art museum.

sections.title: An English landscape garden in the middle of the city
sections.content:
André designed the park in the English landscape style: curving paths, informal clumps of trees, wide sweeping lawns and natural-looking water instead of the rigid geometry of a French formal garden. The result is a park that reads as countryside while sitting inside the built-up upper town.

Mature plane trees, chestnuts and beeches give shade over most of the grounds, the paths are broad and mostly level, and the lawns — above all the Kinnekswiss — provide the open space that is rare this close to a city centre. Sculptures, the orangery and the two villas punctuate the walk without interrupting the green.

sections.title: Everyday life and event venue
sections.content:
For generations the park has been where Luxembourg City meets: lunch breaks on the grass, joggers on the outer loop, families at the playgrounds, students revising under the trees, and open-air culture in summer. It is one of the city's main free cultural venues — the Kinnekswiss hosts concerts, film screenings, the Spillfest children's festival and, in winter, seasonal installations.

Because the park is central, free and easy to reach, it is also a natural starting or ending point for a walking tour of Ville-Haute: the old town, the Grand Ducal Palace and the Pétrusse valley are all within a short walk.

sections.title: A simple walk through the park
sections.content:
Enter from Bd Joseph II, follow the main path past the trees to the Kinnekswiss, continue towards Villa Vauban and the orangery, then loop back past the playgrounds and the bandstand area. At an unhurried pace this takes about an hour; with a picnic or a stop at Villa Vauban, allow two.

Late afternoon is the best time for light and for seeing the park as locals use it. Morning is quieter and cooler in summer. The park is pleasant in every season, but the plane trees and the autumn colours make September and October especially good.

transport.title: How to get there
transport.airportDesc: Take tram T1 directly from the Findel – Luxembourg Airport stop towards the city centre. Ride to Hamilius or Stäreplaz/Étoile and walk 5–10 minutes to the Bd Joseph II entrance — around 30 minutes door to door. Public transport in Luxembourg has been free in standard class since 2020, so no ticket is needed.
transport.selfDriveDesc: Tram T1 crosses the city and stops at Hamilius and Stäreplaz/Étoile, both a short walk from the park. Trams run frequently during the day and the ride is free in standard class.
transport.busDesc: Several city bus lines serve the stops around Bd Royal, Av. Émile Reuter and Hamilius, all within a few minutes' walk of the park entrances. Check mobilitéit.lu or the mobiliteit.lu app for the current line numbers and times.
transport.intercityDesc: The park is a 5-minute walk from Place Guillaume II and about 10 minutes from the Grand Ducal Palace, so it fits naturally into a walking tour of the upper town.
transport.cyclingDesc: Cycle paths and city bike-share docking points are available around the upper town; the park paths are level and easy to ride, though you should walk your bike on the busiest lawn paths.
transport.tipsDesc: Since 2020 buses, trams and standard-class train travel are free throughout Luxembourg for everyone — residents and visitors alike. First class on trains and a few special services remain chargeable.

parking.title: Parking near the park
parking.lead: The park itself sits in a dense central district, so driving is the least convenient option. If you do drive, use one of the city's underground car parks and walk the last few minutes.
items: Hamilius — the closest large car park, a short walk from the park
Royal / Boulevard Royal — convenient for the northern entrances
Glacis — pay-and-display surface car park, used during large events
Beggen parking — park-and-ride style option with tram/bus connection on event days
parking.note: Street parking in Ville-Haute is limited and mostly short-stay. On event days at the Kinnekswiss, the city advises arriving by public transport.

route.title: A one-hour route through the park
route.overview: Enter from Bd Joseph II, walk to the Kinnekswiss, continue to Villa Vauban and the orangery, then loop back past the playgrounds. About 1 hour at an easy pace, 2 hours with a picnic or a museum stop.
steps: Arrive at Hamilius or Stäreplaz/Étoile and walk to the Bd Joseph II entrance
Follow the main path through the mature trees to the Kinnekswiss lawn
Continue to the orangery and the bandstand area
Pass Villa Vauban and Villa Louvigny
Walk back through the playground area and the sculpture garden
Leave towards the old town, Place Guillaume II or the Pétrusse valley
supplements: Keep to the paths where signposted and respect closed lawns during events
Dogs are welcome but must be kept under control; the city asks owners to clean up
Cycling is tolerated on the main paths at walking speed, not across the lawns
Do not pick plants, climb sculptures or light fires
Glass bottles and open barbecues are not part of a normal park picnic here

items.q: Is Parc Municipal de Luxembourg free to enter?
items.a: Yes. The park, its lawns, paths and playgrounds are free and open to everyone. Only the museums and some ticketed events inside the park buildings charge admission.

items.q: What are the opening hours of Parc Municipal de Luxembourg?
items.a: The park grounds are open every day with free access. The city sets seasonal closing times for the playgrounds and closes parts of the Kinnekswiss lawn while events are being set up or run, so check vdl.lu before a late visit.

The Kinnekswiss is the large central meadow of Parc Municipal de Luxembourg. In Luxembourgish the name means "the King's meadow". It is used for picnics, sports and as the city's main open-air event venue.

items.q: How do I get to Parc Municipal de Luxembourg by public transport?
items.a: Take tram T1 to Hamilius or Stäreplaz/Étoile and walk 5–10 minutes to the Bd Joseph II entrance. Several city buses also stop around Bd Royal and Av. Émile Reuter. Public transport in Luxembourg is free in standard class.

items.q: How do I get to the park from Luxembourg Airport?
items.a: Tram T1 runs directly from the Findel – Luxembourg Airport stop into the city centre. Ride to Hamilius or Stäreplaz/Étoile and walk to the park — about 30 minutes in total, and free in standard class.

items.q: Can you have a picnic in Parc Municipal de Luxembourg?
items.a: Yes, picnicking on the lawns is a normal thing to do here, especially on the Kinnekswiss. Bring a blanket, take your rubbish with you and avoid the areas closed for events.

items.q: Is there a playground in the park?
items.a: Yes, the park has children's playgrounds including a well-known pirate-ship structure, plus open lawns for ball games. They are free and open during the city's posted hours.

items.q: Where can I park near Parc Municipal de Luxembourg?
items.a: The closest large option is the Hamilius car park, with Royal and Glacis also within walking distance. Street parking in Ville-Haute is limited and mostly short-stay; on event days public transport is easier.

items.q: How long should I spend in the park?
items.a: An hour is enough for a walk through the grounds; two hours if you picnic or visit Villa Vauban. Combine it with the old town for a half day.

items.q: Are dogs allowed in Parc Municipal de Luxembourg?
items.a: Dogs are allowed but must be kept under control and cleaned up after. They should stay off the playgrounds.

officialManagement.title: Who looks after the park
officialManagement.text:
Parc Municipal de Luxembourg is a public park owned and maintained by the Ville de Luxembourg. The city manages the lawns, playgrounds, trees and the event programme on the Kinnekswiss, and publishes current opening hours, event dates and park rules on vdl.lu.

The park is officially named after its designer, the French landscape architect Édouard André, and was laid out between 1871 and 1878 on the former fortress ramparts cleared after the 1867 Treaty of London.
